text: Text as an array of chars ending in \0, and walking through characters.
A **character array** stores text one character per box, followed by an invisible end marker `'\0'`. You walk it until you meet that marker.
Read a whole line into a char array with `cin.getline(a, 105)`. Size the array one larger than the longest text, for the end marker.
Writing past the end, or forgetting the `'\0'` when you build text yourself, makes `cout << a` print garbage after the text.
Visit each character: test it, change it, count it.
Letters and digits have consecutive codes, so each test is one range comparison. Writing to `s[i]` changes the string itself.
C's `<cctype>` has the same tests ready made: `isupper`, `islower`, `isalpha`, `isdigit`, `isalnum`, `isspace`, plus `toupper` and `tolower`.
Map the letter to 0…25, do the arithmetic, wrap with `% 26`, map back. Shifting backwards can go negative, so add 26 before the last `% 26` (P1914).
`cnt[ch - 'a']++` is a counting array with the **letter as the index**. Ignore letters that never appear when you look for the minimum (P1125).
A letter's value 1 to 26 is `ch - 'A' + 1`. A product of such values mod 47 is kept small with `p = p * v % 47` at every step (P1200).
C has no string type, only char arrays. You will meet them in older solutions and in scanf and printf code.

text: `strlen(a)` in a loop condition recounts the string every round: O(n²). Store it once.
Mixing scanf or printf with cin or cout is only safe without the fast IO line (`fast` in your template).
std::string: reading, the toolkit, searching, conversions, building output.

text: `s.size()` is **unsigned**: on an empty string, `s.size() - 1` is 18446744073709551615, not −1. Write `int(s.size()) - 1`, or check `s.empty()` first.

the rest of the current line

text: After `cin >> x`, the rest of that line is still waiting. The next getline returns it. Fix: one extra getline to throw it away.
Files made on Windows end lines with `\r\n`, and getline keeps the `\r`. Skip it when you count or compare characters (P5015).
`find` returns an unsigned size_t. Compare it with `string::npos`, not with -1.
`<` on strings compares letter by letter, like a dictionary: `"10" < "9"` is true. Convert to numbers first.
To match **whole words** only, lowercase both strings and put a space on both ends of each. Then `" be "` cannot match inside bee or maybe.
`p = find(w, p + 1)` visits every match, overlapping ones too. Use `p + w.size()` when matches must not overlap (P1308).

rows: build a number digit by digit

text: Working on the digits as a string avoids overflow and keeps leading zeros under your control (P1553).
Parsing means walking the text and deciding by what you see. stringstream can split numbers and symbols for you.
When every statement has the same shape, jump by its length: `i += 5` for `x:=y;` (P1597).
A vertical chart is printed top down: row h shows a * for every column whose count is at least h.
Build each row as a string and trim trailing spaces before printing (P1598).
To glue strings into the smallest result, put x first when `x + y < y + x`. The `[](…) {…}` is a small inline comparison function, a lambda (P1603).
Files with fstream, and redirection on the command line.
Normally a program reads the keyboard and prints to the screen. Files can take their place: either the program opens them itself, or the command line **redirects** the keyboard and screen.
An ifstream is used exactly like cin, and an ofstream exactly like cout. Only the name changes.

rows: cin reads in.txt instead of the keyboard
cout writes to out.txt instead of the screen
compare with the answer (diff on Linux)

text: Redirection needs no code changes, so it is the quickest way to rerun a long sample. Compare outputs with fc or diff, not by eye.
Some contests name the input and output files. Then `freopen` from C reconnects cin and cout to those files, at the start of main.
Comment out freopen when testing by hand, or the program waits on a file. Luogu reads standard input: submit without freopen unless the problem asks for files.
